questions.question: A city council's IT team wants staff sign-in to count as true multifactor authentication (MFA). Which combination BEST meets that goal?

options.A: A password followed by the answer to a security question
options.B: A smart card followed by a code from a phone app
options.C: A password followed by a code from a phone app
options.D: A PIN followed by a long memorized passphrase

questions.key_concept: MFA needs proof from at least two different categories: something you know, something you have and something you are.
questions.pre_read: Read each option step by step and sort every step into know, have or are.
questions.correct_explanation: A password is something you know and a code from an app on the user's phone proves something you have, so the pair spans two categories and counts as MFA. The smart card and phone app look stronger because there are two devices, but both are things you have. Two items from one category add a step, not a second factor, however many devices are involved.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it adds a second check. But a security answer is another memorized secret, so both steps are something you know, and the answers are often guessable.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: two devices feel twice as strong. But the card and the phone are both things you have, and two of one category do not make MFA.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because a long passphrase is a strong secret. But a PIN and a passphrase are both things you know, so the sign-in still uses one category.

tips: Eliminate: A and D pair two memorized secrets; a security answer or a passphrase is still something you know.
Final two: C beats B because a password and an app code come from two categories, while a card and a phone app are both things you have.
Exam cue: label every step know, have or are. MFA needs two different labels, not two steps.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-63B-4 (Authentication and Authenticator Management: multi-factor authentication); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 IA-2 (Identification and Authentication (Organizational Users))
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'MFA counts factor categories, not steps' (notes 3.1.4 Authentication Factors and MFA). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 pilot batch, 28 Oct 2026. Audit fix 28 Oct 2026: key changed from fingerprint to app code so it matches the 800-63B-4 rule that biometrics pair with a physical authenticator.

questions.question: A hospital's IT team wants administrators to use a sign-in method that a fake login page cannot capture and replay. Which method BEST fits?

options.A: A one-time code sent to the administrator's phone by text
options.B: A long passphrase checked against a list of breached passwords
options.C: A push approval in an app that uses number matching
options.D: A passkey stored on a hardware security key

questions.key_concept: Phishing-resistant methods such as passkeys bind each sign-in to the genuine site, so a fake page gets nothing it can reuse.
questions.pre_read: Picture the fake login page in the stem, and note what each method would hand over to it.
questions.correct_explanation: A passkey signs a challenge from the real site, and the browser checks the site's address, so a look-alike page gets nothing it can replay. Number matching is the runner-up: it stops blind approvals by tired users, but a fake page can show the user the real site's number and pass the approval straight through.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because texted codes are a familiar second step. But a fake page can collect and relay one, and a subscriber identity module (SIM) swap can redirect it.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a breach-screened passphrase is a strong secret. But it is still one typed factor, and the user can type it straight into a fake page.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: number matching defeats careless approvals. But a fake page can display the real site's number, so the relayed sign-in still succeeds.

tips: Eliminate: A sends a code that a look-alike page can collect and relay, and B is a single typed secret that phishing captures.
Final two: D beats C because a passkey works only on the genuine site; number matching stops blind approvals, not a relayed sign-in.
Exam cue: when the threat is a fake login page, choose a site-bound method such as a passkey on a phone or a hardware security key.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-63B-4 (Authentication and Authenticator Management: phishing resistance); CIS Controls v8.1 Safeguard 6.5 (Require MFA for Administrative Access)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'only site-bound authenticators resist a relayed fake login page' (notes 3.1.5 Phishing-Resistant MFA and Passkeys). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 pilot batch, 28 Oct 2026.

questions.question: A help desk technician notes the password standard, owned by the security manager, forces a change every 60 days, against current National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) guidance. What is the technician's BEST action?

options.A: Turn off password expiry in the directory to match the guidance
options.B: Shorten the change interval to 30 days to compensate
options.C: Propose the change to the owner of the password rules
options.D: Add a symbol rule to make each new password stronger

questions.key_concept: Exact password settings live in a standard that security management approves; practitioners propose changes to its owner.
questions.pre_read: Note who is acting and who owns the standard. Then read what each option would change, and where.
questions.correct_explanation: Current NIST guidance drops scheduled password changes, so the standard is out of date, but the technician does not own it. Proposing the change to the owner puts it in front of the people who approve the standard. Turning off expiry directly has the right goal, but it changes live settings without approval and leaves the written standard and the systems out of step.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the goal matches current guidance. But changing live settings is outside a technician's role and bypasses the security manager, who approves the standard.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because more frequent changes sound stricter. But they push users toward predictable patterns; NIST advises a change on evidence of compromise, not on a calendar.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because a symbol looks like extra strength. But composition rules lead to predictable patterns; NIST favors length and breach screening over character mixes.

tips: Eliminate: B makes forced changes more frequent and D adds a character rule; current NIST guidance drops both in favor of length and breach screening.
Final two: C beats A because the technician does not own the standard; its owner approves the change before live settings move.
Exam cue: when you spot an outdated rule you do not own, take it to the owner rather than changing production yourself.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-63B-4 (Authentication and Authenticator Management: password requirements); ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Control 5.17 (Authentication information)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'practitioners route changes to a standard through its owner' (notes 3.1.6 Passwords and Modern Password Standards). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 pilot batch, 28 Oct 2026.

questions.question: A senior manager phones the help desk to request an account for a consultant starting today, but no human resources (HR) start record exists. What should the technician do FIRST?

options.A: Create the account now and ask HR to add the record later
options.B: Copy the access the project owner gave another consultant
options.C: Create the account with broad access and trim it later
options.D: Refer it to the access team, since accounts follow HR records

questions.key_concept: Accounts are created from a trusted record, such as an HR start record; urgency or seniority never replaces that trigger.
questions.pre_read: Look for what normally triggers a new account, and check whether it is present here. Note who is applying the pressure.
questions.correct_explanation: Provisioning starts from a trusted record, and here there is none, so the technician refers the request to the access team instead of creating anything. Creating the account first and fixing the record later is the runner-up: it feels helpful, but it hands working credentials to an identity nobody has checked, and urgency from a senior caller is a classic social engineering pressure.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: it feels helpful, and the record may follow. But without it nobody has confirmed the consultant exists or what they need, and the caller could be an impostor.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the project owner approved that access. But it was approved for someone else and may carry leftover rights; access comes from an approved role once a record exists.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it avoids day-one delays. But broad access is live at once and the trimming rarely happens; start with the smallest fitting role after the record exists.

tips: Eliminate: B copies another person's rights, which may include leftovers, and C grants broad access first; both break least privilege at provisioning.
Final two: D beats A because no trusted record means no account yet; the access team, not the caller's urgency, decides how to proceed.
Exam cue: no record, no account. Pressure from rank or a deadline is a reason to follow the process, not to skip it.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-2 (Account Management); ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Control 5.16 (Identity management)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'no trusted record, no account' (notes 3.1.3 Provisioning and Identity Proofing). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 pilot batch, 28 Oct 2026.

questions.question: A charity is moving its email, files and donor database behind single sign-on (SSO) with one identity provider. Which protection is MOST important for the IT team to add?

options.A: Strong multifactor authentication and monitoring at the identity provider
options.B: A separate local password on each app for backup
options.C: Strong multifactor authentication on the donor database, the most sensitive app
options.D: Longer identity provider sessions so staff sign in less often

questions.key_concept: SSO concentrates risk at the identity provider, so it needs the strongest authentication and monitoring.
questions.pre_read: Trace how staff reach email, files and the donor database after the move, and where each option adds protection.
questions.correct_explanation: With SSO, every app trusts the identity provider, so it is the one front door to everything. Strong multifactor authentication (MFA) and monitoring there protects email, files and the donor database at once. Guarding only the donor database is the runner-up: it shields one app, but a stolen identity provider login would still open the rest.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a backup login sounds resilient. But local passwords bypass SSO, giving attackers a second way in that disabling the user at the identity provider will not close.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: the donor database is the most sensitive app. But with SSO, an attacker who takes over the identity provider login still reaches email and files.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because fewer prompts feel convenient. But longer sessions widen the window in which a stolen session can be used; they reduce prompts, not risk.

tips: Eliminate: B adds local logins that bypass SSO, and D lengthens sessions, which widens the window for a stolen session.
Final two: A beats C because every app trusts the identity provider; protecting one app leaves the shared front door weaker.
Exam cue: with SSO, protect the identity provider hardest. A control on one app cannot cover the rest.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-63C-4 (Federation and Assertions); CIS Controls v8.1 Safeguard 6.7 (Centralize Access Control)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'SSO concentrates risk at the identity provider' (notes 3.1.7 Single Sign-On and Federation). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 pilot batch, 28 Oct 2026.

questions.question: A sales manager, who is accountable for the team's access, asks the analyst running the quarterly access review to let each salesperson confirm their own access. What is the analyst's BEST response?

options.A: Agree with the manager, and send each salesperson their access to confirm
options.B: Keep the review with the manager, who must confirm each line
options.C: Approve any lines nobody confirms to close the review on time
options.D: Ask IT to confirm the access from recent usage logs

questions.key_concept: Access reviews are done by the accountable manager or data owner, never by the person whose access is reviewed.
questions.pre_read: Note who is accountable for the team's access, and who each option would make the reviewer.
questions.correct_explanation: A review works only when someone accountable for the work, with no stake in the result, decides each line; here that is the manager. Usage logs are the runner-up: they show what people use, not what their job needs, and IT does not own that business decision, so access that is used but unneeded would pass.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because each salesperson knows what they use. But reviewing your own access is a conflict of interest, and people tend to keep everything; the accountable manager confirms it.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it meets the deadline. But access nobody confirms should be removed, not approved; approving unanswered lines defeats the purpose of the review.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: logs are objective evidence of use. But they show what is used, not what is needed, and IT is not accountable for the team's access.

tips: Eliminate: A has people certify their own access, a conflict of interest, and C approves unanswered lines, when unconfirmed access should be removed.
Final two: B beats D because the accountable manager decides what the job needs; usage logs and IT cannot make that business call.
Exam cue: in an access review, look for the accountable owner with no stake in the result. Unconfirmed access is removed.
questions.framework_ref: ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Control 5.18 (Access rights); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-2 (Account Management)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'the accountable owner, not the user, certifies access' (notes 3.1.10 Access Reviews and Recertification). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 pilot batch, 28 Oct 2026.

questions.question: Human resources (HR) has scheduled a contractor's exit meeting for 3 p.m., and the manager fears the contractor may cause harm. What should the IT technician do FIRST?

options.A: Reset the contractor's password and leave the account active
options.B: Delete the account and mailbox as the meeting starts
options.C: Disable the account and end its sessions as the meeting starts
options.D: Disable the account and end its sessions after the meeting

questions.key_concept: For a hostile exit, access is cut as the person is told; disable first and delete later so logs stay traceable.
questions.pre_read: Note the risk signal in the scenario, then compare what each option does and when.
questions.correct_explanation: When a leaver may cause harm, access is cut as they are told, leaving no window to retaliate. Disabling keeps the account for logs and data, and ending sessions stops sign-ins already open. Acting after the meeting is the runner-up: the steps are right, but the contractor keeps working access while they hear the news.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because a reset blocks the old password. But open sessions and tokens can survive it, and the account itself stays live.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because deleting removes access completely. But it can lose data the firm needs and breaks the link between logs and the person; disable now, delete later.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: the steps are right, but the timing is wrong. During the meeting the contractor still has working access and a reason to misuse it.

tips: Eliminate: A only resets the password, so open sessions survive, and B deletes the account, losing data and the trail that ties logs to the person.
Final two: C beats D because a hostile exit needs access cut as the news is given; after the meeting is too late.
Exam cue: for leavers, disable rather than delete, revoke sessions too, and match the timing to the risk.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 PS-4 (Personnel Termination); CIS Controls v8.1 Safeguard 6.2 (Establish an Access Revoking Process)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'hostile exits: disable and revoke sessions as the person is told' (notes 3.1.11 Deprovisioning Leavers). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 pilot batch, 28 Oct 2026. Review fixes 29 Oct 2026 (standards audit 2 and blind test 2): D shortened by one word so the key is the wordiest option.

questions.question: An email that seems to be from a department head asks a help desk analyst to add an intern to the team drive today, without a ticket. What should the analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Add the intern now on the department head's authority
options.B: Reply to the email asking the sender to confirm
options.C: Call the department head on the number in the directory
options.D: Give the intern read-only access until a ticket arrives

questions.key_concept: Unusual or urgent access requests are verified through a channel already on file, never the channel the request came in on.
questions.pre_read: Note how the request arrived and what normal paperwork is missing from it.
questions.correct_explanation: Email is easy to fake, so the analyst first confirms the request through a channel already on file, here the directory number. Even once confirmed, access waits for a ticket. Replying to the email is the runner-up: it looks like verification, but the reply goes to whoever sent the message, so an impostor simply confirms their own request.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because a department head can usually approve access. But rank is no substitute for a recorded approval, and the email may be forged.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: it looks like checking. But a reply goes back to the sender, so if the email is forged, the impostor simply confirms it.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because read-only feels like a safe middle ground. But it can still expose sensitive files, and any grant needs an approved request first.

tips: Eliminate: A treats the sender's rank as an approval, and D grants partial access before any approved request exists.
Final two: C beats B because a callback uses a channel already on file; a reply goes straight back to a possible impostor.
Exam cue: verify an unusual request through a known channel, never the one the request arrived on.
questions.framework_ref: CIS Controls v8.1 Safeguard 6.1 (Establish an Access Granting Process); ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Control 5.18 (Access rights)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'verify unusual requests through a channel already on file' (notes 3.1.14 Access Requests and Approvals). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 pilot batch, 28 Oct 2026. questions.question: A buyer who raises purchase orders moves to accounts payable, which releases supplier payments, and keeps their purchasing rights. What is the access analyst's BEST action?

options.A: Leave the old purchasing rights in place until the next access review
options.B: Have the data owner review the buyer's payments each month
options.C: Let the buyer keep the old rights to help their former team
options.D: Request removal of the old rights and alert the data owner

questions.key_concept: A transfer is a leaver plus a joiner: remove old access at the move, especially where old and new rights conflict.
questions.pre_read: Combine the buyer's old and new rights, and note what one person could now do alone.
questions.correct_explanation: Purchasing rights in a payments job let one person raise an order and pay it, a separation of duties conflict. The mover process removes old access at the move, and the data owner decides on any handover need. A monthly owner review of the payments is the runner-up: it is a compensating control for when duties cannot be split, but here they can.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because reviews exist to catch leftover access. But they are a backstop, often months apart; the conflict is live today, so old access goes at the move.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: an owner's monthly review is a real compensating control. But it only detects misuse after payment, and it suits teams too small to split duties.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because helping a former team sounds cooperative. But that is a handover need, approved separately with an end date; keeping full rights builds privilege creep.

tips: Eliminate: A waits for a review that may be months away, and C keeps old rights for convenience, which is privilege creep.
Final two: D beats B because removing the old rights prevents the conflict; a report only detects misuse and suits duties that cannot be split.
Exam cue: when a mover's old and new rights let one person start and finish a payment, remove the old access before reaching for monitoring.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 PS-5 (Personnel Transfer); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-5 (Separation of Duties)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'a transfer is a leaver plus a joiner; remove conflicting old access at the move' (notes 3.1.9 Movers and Privilege Creep). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 pilot batch, 28 Oct 2026.

questions.question: A junior engineer finds the application programming interface (API) key for the company's AI chatbot, which the platform team owns, pasted in a busy team chat channel. What should the engineer do FIRST?

options.A: Report it to the security team, since copies may exist
options.B: Post a reminder in the team channel not to share keys
options.C: Delete the chat message so nobody else can copy it
options.D: Revoke the key at once in the cloud console

questions.key_concept: An exposed secret is a security event: report it so the security team and the key's owner can rotate it and check for misuse.
questions.pre_read: Note who owns the key, what depends on it, and who is acting.
questions.correct_explanation: An exposed key may already be copied, so the security team needs to know at once: it can bring in the platform team, rotate the key without breaking the chatbot and check logs for misuse. Revoking it alone is the runner-up: speed matters, but the engineer does not own the key, and pulling it unannounced can break a live service and skip the check for misuse.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it may prevent the next leak. But this key is already exposed and still works.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it stops more people from seeing the key. But anyone who copied it can still use it; the key stays valid until it is rotated.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: speed matters with a leaked key. But the platform team owns it; revoking it unannounced can break the live chatbot and skip the check for misuse.

tips: Eliminate: B addresses future habits, not a secret already exposed, and C removes the message but leaves a copied key valid.
Final two: A beats D because the platform team, not the engineer, owns the key; the security team coordinates rotation with its owner and checks for misuse.
Exam cue: when you find a leaked password, key or token you do not own, report it at once rather than fixing it alone.
questions.framework_ref: OWASP Non-Human Identities Top 10 (2025) NHI2 (Secret Leakage); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 IA-5 (Authenticator Management)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'a leaked machine secret is reported so its owner and security can rotate it' (notes 3.1.12 Non-Human Identities Through the Life Cycle). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 pilot batch, 28 Oct 2026. Review fixes 28 Oct 2026 (blind test and standards audit). Stem now states that the platform team owns the key.

questions.question: A temporary worker signs in with multifactor authentication (MFA) and can then open every client folder on the file server. Which part of access control has MOST clearly failed?

options.A: Identification, because the worker's username is not unique
options.B: Authorization, because the worker's rights exceed their job
options.C: Authentication, because the sign-in should be stronger
options.D: Accounting, because the folder opens were not logged

questions.key_concept: Authentication proves who someone is; authorization limits what they may do. Strong sign-in cannot fix overly broad permissions.
questions.pre_read: Notice which steps of the sign-in worked and what happened next. Then name the step behind the problem.
questions.correct_explanation: The worker proved who they were with MFA, so authentication worked. The failure is authorization: the file server let a correctly identified person open folders their job does not need. Stronger sign-in is the runner-up only because MFA feels like the fix; it would let the same person in with the same broad rights.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because identification is the first step of access. But nothing points to a shared or duplicate username; the worker was identified, and the problem is what they could open.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: MFA is the usual fix for access problems. But MFA already proved who the worker is; stronger sign-in cannot limit which folders they open.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because accounting is part of access control too. But logging records what happened without deciding access; full logs would still leave every folder open.

tips: Eliminate: A blames identification with no sign of a shared username, and D names logging, which records access but does not grant or block it.
Final two: B beats C because the worker's identity was proved; the failure is in what that identity was allowed to open.
Exam cue: if the right person reaches the wrong data, the fault is authorization, not authentication.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-3 (Access Enforcement); ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Control 5.15 (Access control)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'authentication proves identity; authorization limits access' (notes 3.2.1 Logical Access Controls and Access Decisions). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 pilot batch, 28 Oct 2026.

questions.question: A new reporting tool's service account must read last month's sales tables each night to build a dashboard. Which access is BEST for the database owner to approve?

options.A: Read access to the sales tables this job uses
options.B: The administrator rights listed in the vendor's setup guide
options.C: Read and write access, in case the reports need fixes
options.D: Read access to the sales tables and the rest of the database

questions.key_concept: Least privilege limits both the kind of access and its scope: only the actions and data the task needs.
questions.pre_read: List what the nightly job does and which data it touches, then compare each option with that list.
questions.correct_explanation: The job only reads the sales tables the dashboard uses, so read access to those tables is enough. Read access to every table is the runner-up: it is read-only, but least privilege limits scope as well as action, and wider reach means a stolen service account exposes far more data.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the vendor knows its own tool. But a setup guide is not a task need, and administrator rights would let a stolen service account change or delete everything.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because fixes may be needed one day. But the task never writes, so write access only adds risk; fixing reports is a separate request.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: read-only is right, but the scope is too wide. The nightly job needs a few tables, not the whole database.

tips: Eliminate: B grants the administrator rights a vendor's guide lists, and C adds write access the nightly job never uses.
Final two: A beats D because least privilege limits scope as well as action; the whole database is more than the dashboard needs.
Exam cue: match access to the exact task, both what it does and which data it touches. 'Just in case' is not a need.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-6 (Least Privilege); ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Control 5.15 (Access control)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'least privilege limits scope as well as action, for automated accounts too' (notes 3.2.2 Least Privilege and Need to Know). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 pilot batch, 28 Oct 2026.

questions.question: At a small software firm, one developer writes code and also releases it to production, and hiring a second developer is not possible. Which control BEST reduces the risk?

options.A: Rely on the developer's long record of reliable work
options.B: Have someone without release rights approve each release
options.C: Cut the developer's rights to the minimum they need
options.D: Give the developer a separate account for releases

questions.key_concept: Where one person must hold conflicting duties, an independent check by someone else is the compensating control.
questions.pre_read: Notice what one person can do from start to finish here. Ask which option actually changes that.
questions.correct_explanation: Writing and releasing code are conflicting duties, and the firm cannot split them by hiring. Approval by someone with no release rights adds the independent check that separation of duties needs. Cutting rights to the minimum is the runner-up: least privilege is good practice, but the developer's minimum still includes writing and releasing, so the conflict remains.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because a proven record feels like assurance. But separation of duties is not about distrust; it protects the firm and the developer alike, and a good record prevents nothing.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: least privilege is sound practice. But it limits how much one person can do; here the minimum still includes both writing and releasing.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because a separate release account looks like a split. But both accounts belong to the same person, who can still write and release a change alone.

tips: Eliminate: A relies on trust, which separation of duties is designed not to need, and D gives the same person a second account, so nothing is split.
Final two: B beats C because the conflict is between duties, not the amount of access; only a second person breaks it.
Exam cue: when one person can start and finish a sensitive task, look for an independent second person, even as a compensating check.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-5 (Separation of Duties); ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Control 5.3 (Segregation of duties)

Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 pilot batch, 28 Oct 2026.

questions.question: At a logistics firm, IT administrators read email and browse the web while signed in with their domain administrator accounts. Which change should the IT manager make to BEST reduce this risk?

options.A: Require a longer password on each domain administrator account
options.B: Give administrators separate standard accounts for daily work
options.C: Install a stronger web filter on the administrators' computers
options.D: Log every website visited from the administrator accounts

questions.key_concept: Administrators use a separate standard account for everyday work, so a phishing email or bad website never runs with admin rights.
questions.pre_read: Note what the administrators do while signed in to their powerful accounts, and what each option changes about that.
questions.correct_explanation: Email and web browsing are where much malware and phishing arrive. Done under a domain administrator account, one bad click runs with rights over the whole network. A separate standard account for daily work means a bad click gets only ordinary rights; the admin account is used only for admin tasks. A web filter is the runner-up: it blocks some bad sites but leaves every miss running as an administrator.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because admin accounts deserve strong passwords. But malware from a bad link runs under the signed-in account, so it still gets domain administrator rights.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: filtering blocks some bad sites. But no filter catches everything, and whatever gets through still runs with domain administrator rights.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because logging adds visibility. But it blocks nothing; a malicious page would still run with administrator rights before anyone reads the log.

tips: Eliminate: A strengthens a password the attack never needs to guess, and D only records visits after the harm is done.
Final two: B beats C because a separate daily account removes admin rights from risky work; a filter only lowers the odds of a bad click.
Exam cue: admin accounts are for admin tasks only. Everyday email and browsing belong to a standard account.
questions.framework_ref: CIS Controls v8.1 Safeguard 5.4 (Restrict Administrator Privileges to Dedicated Administrator Accounts); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-6(2) (Least Privilege | Non-privileged Access for Nonsecurity Functions)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'administrators keep a separate standard account for everyday work' (notes 3.2.4 Privileged Access Management). Replaces the shared-admin-login version, which duplicated cc_d1_003. Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 pilot audit fix, 28 Oct 2026.

questions.question: A project lead creates a budget folder and chooses to share it with the Finance group, giving that group edit rights. Which access control model does this BEST describe?

options.A: Discretionary access control, because the owner decides
options.B: Role-based access control, because the owner shares with a group
options.C: Mandatory access control, because labels set by the system decide
options.D: Rule-based access control, because one fixed rule covers everyone

questions.key_concept: Name the model by who decides: when the resource owner chooses who gets access, it is discretionary, even if they choose a group.
questions.pre_read: Find who chose the access in the scenario and how they made the choice.
questions.correct_explanation: The project lead created the folder and personally chose who could edit it, so the owner decides: discretionary access control. Role-based control is the runner-up because a group is involved, but in role-based access control (RBAC) the organization assigns permissions to job roles through an approved process; here the owner simply picked a group to share with.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: a group sounds like a role. But in RBAC the organization sets role permissions centrally; here the folder's owner chose the group.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because shared folders often carry labels. But mandatory control relies on labels and clearances set centrally, and owners cannot share at will under it.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because sharing settings look like a rule. But rule-based control applies one administrator rule to every request; here one person chose whom to share with.

tips: Eliminate: C needs labels and clearances, and D needs one administrator rule for everyone; the scenario shows neither.
Final two: A beats B because the folder's owner picked the group; role-based access is set centrally by job role.
Exam cue: name the model by its decider. An owner choosing, even choosing a group, means discretionary.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-3(4) (Access Enforcement | Discretionary Access Control); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-3(7) (Access Enforcement | Role-based Access Control)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'the owner deciding, even by choosing a group, is discretionary' (notes 3.2.5 Discretionary Access Control (DAC)). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 pilot batch, 28 Oct 2026.

questions.question: A Secret-cleared government analyst tries to send part of a Secret report to a lower-cleared partner agency, but the system blocks it under labels the security officer sets. What is the analyst's BEST next step?

options.A: Ask their manager to approve an exception to the block
options.B: Ask the security officer to review that part for release
options.C: Relabel the part the analyst wrote, then tell the security officer
options.D: Retype that part into a new document without a label

questions.key_concept: Under mandatory access control, central labels and clearances decide; only the central security authority approves releasing data to a lower level.
questions.pre_read: Note which model the system uses and who sets its labels.
questions.correct_explanation: Under mandatory access control (MAC), labels and releases are set by a central security authority, not by users or line managers, so the analyst asks the security officer to review that part for an authorized release. Asking a manager is the runner-up: escalating is the right instinct, but a manager has no authority to override labels the system enforces.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: escalating is the right instinct, but to the wrong person. Under MAC a line manager cannot override labels; the central security authority approves releases.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it keeps the security officer informed. But under MAC, writing text gives no control over its label; the security officer decides before anything changes.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it gets the work done. But copying data into an unlabeled document bypasses the control; it is a security violation, whatever the intent.

tips: Eliminate: C changes a label the analyst has no authority over, even with notice afterward, and D copies the data around the label; MAC permits neither.
Final two: B beats A because only the central security authority can approve a release; a manager cannot override the system's labels.
Exam cue: under mandatory access control, route any change to labels, clearances or releases to the central security authority.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-3(3) (Access Enforcement | Mandatory Access Control); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-16 (Security and Privacy Attributes)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'under MAC only the central security authority approves releases' (notes 3.2.6 Mandatory Access Control (MAC)). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 pilot batch, 28 Oct 2026. Review fixes 28 Oct 2026 (blind test and standards audit). Stem now names the lower-cleared partner and who sets the labels.

questions.question: A hospital's IT team must let nurses open charts only for patients on their own ward, from hospital devices, during their shift. Which access control model BEST fits?

options.A: Role-based access control, with a role for each combination
options.B: Mandatory access control, with a clearance for each nurse
options.C: Discretionary access control, with each ward manager setting rights
options.D: Attribute-based access control, with a policy checking each request

questions.key_concept: When access depends on several conditions at once, such as who, where and when, attribute-based access control fits best.
questions.pre_read: Count the conditions each access decision depends on. Then ask how each model would express them.
questions.correct_explanation: Each decision depends on several attributes at once: the nurse's ward, the device and the time. Attribute-based access control (ABAC) checks a policy against those attributes on every request, so one policy covers every combination. Role-based control is the runner-up: a Nurse role fits the job, but ward, device and shift would need a role per combination, and plain roles cannot check time or device.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: nurses clearly share a job role. But roles capture job function, not changing conditions; a role per ward, device and shift would multiply beyond control.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because patient records are highly sensitive. But clearances and labels protect classified data; they cannot express ward, device or shift conditions.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because ward managers know their own staff. But under discretionary control owners share at will, so nothing would enforce the conditions consistently.

tips: Eliminate: B uses clearances and labels meant for classified data, and C leaves managers to set rights, so nothing enforces the conditions.
Final two: D beats A because one attribute policy covers every ward, device and shift; roles would need one per combination.
Exam cue: several conditions at once, such as who, where, when and on what device, point to attribute-based access control.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-162 (Guide to Attribute Based Access Control (ABAC) Definition and Considerations); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-3(13) (Access Enforcement | Attribute-based Access Control)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'several conditions at once point to ABAC' (notes 3.2.8 Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC)). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 pilot batch, 28 Oct 2026.

questions.question: At a university, staff reach the student records system according to their job, and nobody can sign in to it from outside the country. Which description should the security team record as MOST accurate?

options.A: Role-based for the job access and rule-based for the country block
options.B: Role-based for both the job access and the country block
options.C: Discretionary for the job access and rule-based for the country block
options.D: Role-based for the job access and mandatory for the country block

questions.key_concept: Real systems often mix models; split the scenario and name the model for each part by its decider.
questions.pre_read: Split the scenario into its two controls, and name the decider for each one separately.
questions.correct_explanation: Access that follows each person's job is role-based. The country block applies one fixed rule to everyone, whatever their job, so it is rule-based, layered on top. Calling both role-based is the runner-up, because the names sound alike. If the decision combined several attributes per request, such as job, device and time, it would be attribute-based.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: role-based and rule-based sound alike. But the country block applies to everyone regardless of role, so it is rule-based.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the country half is right. But job-based access is set by the organization through roles, not chosen by each owner.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the job half is right and a hard block feels mandatory. But the country block uses no labels or clearances, so it is not mandatory access control.

tips: Eliminate: C treats job-based access as owner-chosen, and D treats a location block as label-based; each gets one part wrong.
Final two: A beats B because the country block applies to everyone, whatever their job; that makes it rule-based, not role-based.
Exam cue: when two models seem to fit, split the scenario and name the model for each part by who or what decides.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-3 (Access Enforcement); CIS Controls v8.1 Safeguard 6.8 (Define and Maintain Role-Based Access Control)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'split a mixed scenario and name the model for each part' (notes 3.2.13 Access Model Scenarios: Worked Examples). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 pilot batch, 28 Oct 2026.

questions.subtopic: 3.2 Logical access. Automated systems and AI agents
questions.question: An online retailer's AI agent reads complaints and drafts refunds, and its vendor wants it to pay refunds of any size directly. Which setup is BEST for the security analyst to propose?

options.A: Let the agent pay refunds under the support manager's login
options.B: Give the agent the full finance access the vendor requests
options.C: Let the agent draft refunds for a person to approve
options.D: Let the agent pay refunds and review its logs each month

questions.key_concept: AI agents get least privilege and cannot finish high-impact actions alone; a person approves payments, deletions and similar steps.
questions.pre_read: Note where the agent's input comes from, and what each option lets it do with money.
questions.correct_explanation: An agent that reads customer complaints can be misled by crafted text, and a paid refund is hard to undo, so the agent drafts and a person approves before money moves. Monthly log review is the runner-up: logging the agent's actions is good practice, but it finds a bad refund weeks after it is paid, not before.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it works at once with no setup. But a borrowed login gives the agent all the manager's rights and makes its actions look like the manager's.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the vendor knows its agent. But a vendor's request is not a task need; broad finance access lets a manipulated or faulty agent do far more harm.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: logging the agent is good practice. But monthly review finds bad refunds long after the money has gone; payments need approval before they happen.

tips: Eliminate: A lends the agent a person's login, and B grants the broad access a vendor asks for; both break least privilege for agents.
Final two: C beats D because human approval stops a bad payment before it happens; a monthly log review only finds it afterward.
Exam cue: for AI agents and bots, high-impact actions such as payments get a human approval step, not just an after-the-fact review.
questions.framework_ref: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025 LLM06 (Excessive Agency); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-6 (Least Privilege)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'AI agents cannot finish high-impact actions alone; a human approves before money moves' (notes 3.2.11 Least Privilege and SoD for Automated Systems and AI Agents). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 pilot batch, 28 Oct 2026.

questions.question: A hospital's server team wants permanent domain administrator rights so they can respond quickly to overnight outages. Which approach BEST balances speed and risk?

options.A: Give every admin permanent rights protected by a long password
options.B: Share one admin login among the night team for emergencies
options.C: Give on-call admins standing rights for their whole shift
options.D: Grant rights just in time for each approved task, with logging

questions.key_concept: Privileged rights should be borrowed for an approved task and then expire; standing rights help attackers around the clock.
questions.pre_read: For each option, note who holds admin rights and for how long.
questions.correct_explanation: Just-in-time access switches admin rights on for an approved task, logs the session and lets the rights expire, so they exist only while needed. Shift-long rights are the runner-up: they cut exposure compared with permanent rights, but they stay live for hours with no task, which is still standing privilege an attacker can use.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because a long password sounds protective. But permanent rights are open to attackers around the clock, and a password alone does not protect powerful accounts well enough.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because one login is fast in an emergency. But a shared login hides who acted, and its password spreads to everyone on the team.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: shift-long rights cut exposure compared with permanent ones. But they stay live for hours with no task; rights tied to an approved task expire sooner.

tips: Eliminate: A keeps permanent rights behind a password, the standing exposure to avoid, and B shares one admin login, so no action traces to one person.
Final two: D beats C because rights tied to an approved task expire when the work ends; shift-long rights sit idle for hours.
Exam cue: for admin access, prefer rights that are requested, approved, logged and expire over rights that are always on.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-6 (Least Privilege); ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Control 8.2 (Privileged access rights)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'privilege is borrowed for an approved task, then expires' (notes 3.2.12 Just-in-Time and Break-Glass Access). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 pilot batch, 28 Oct 2026. Review fixes 29 Oct 2026 (standards audit 2 and blind test 2): C shortened so the key is the wordiest option.

questions.subtopic: 3.1 Identity life cycle. Identities and accounts
questions.question: A marketing team's new AI agent will post scheduled social media updates, and the team lead wants it to run under the lead's own account. Which setup is BEST for the IT analyst to propose?

options.A: One shared team account for the agent and the staff
options.B: A separate account, with an owner and rights to post only
options.C: The lead's account, with every post the agent makes logged
options.D: An administrator account, so permission errors cannot stop posts

questions.key_concept: Every identity, including an AI agent or other non-human one, needs its own account so actions trace to the right actor.
questions.pre_read: Ask whose name the logs would show for each setup, and what else each account could do.
questions.correct_explanation: Every identity, human or machine, should be unique, so each action traces to the right actor. The agent gets its own account with a named owner and only the rights it needs to post. Running it under the lead's account, even with logging, is the runner-up: the logs would show the lead acting, and the agent would hold all of the lead's rights.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because one account is simple to manage. But a shared account hides whether a person or the agent acted, so nobody can be held to account.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: logging adds a record. But every post would look like the lead's own, and the agent would carry all of the lead's rights.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it avoids failed posts. But administrator rights go far beyond posting, so a faulty or misused agent could change almost anything.

tips: Eliminate: A puts the agent and staff on one login that cannot show who acted, and D gives a posting tool administrator rights it does not need.
Final two: B beats C because a separate account shows what the agent did; on the lead's account, its actions look like the lead's and it holds all their rights.
Exam cue: bots, scripts and AI agents each get their own identity, a human owner and only the rights the task needs.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 IA-4 (Identifier Management); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-2 (Account Management)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'each person or system, including an AI agent, gets its own unique identity' (notes 3.1.1 Identities, Accounts and the Life Cycle). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 2, 30 Oct 2026.

questions.question: A transit agency's IT analyst is building a 'fare inspector' role; the head of revenue owns the ticketing data, and the security manager checks roles for conflicts. Who should MOST appropriately approve the role's permissions?

options.A: The IT analyst building the role
options.B: The security manager
options.C: The ticketing system's vendor
options.D: The head of revenue

questions.key_concept: The business or data owner approves what a role contains; IT builds the role and security advises.
questions.pre_read: Read each option as a person, and ask what each one knows about the work and answers for.
questions.correct_explanation: The head of revenue owns the data and knows what inspectors need, so they approve the role's contents; IT builds it. The security manager is the runner-up: checking new roles for separation of duties conflicts is a real part of the process, but that check advises the owner; it does not decide what inspectors need.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the analyst knows the system best. But building and approving the same role removes the check, and IT does not own the work.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the security manager does check new roles. But that check looks for conflicts and advises; the data owner decides what inspectors need.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because vendors ship default roles. But defaults rarely match one agency's duties, and the vendor is not accountable for the data.

tips: Eliminate: A would approve their own build, and C is not accountable for the agency's data or duties.
Final two: D beats B because the data owner decides what the job needs; the security manager checks for conflicts and advises.
Exam cue: owners approve, IT builds, security advises. When asked who approves access, look for the owner of the data or process.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-2 (Account Management); CIS Controls v8.1 Safeguard 6.8 (Define and Maintain Role-Based Access Control)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'the business or data owner approves what a role contains' (notes 3.1.2 Defining Roles and Entitlements). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 2, 30 Oct 2026.

questions.question: A college's AI sign-in model scores a lecturer's attempt as medium risk: the password is right, but the laptop is unfamiliar. Which response BEST fits risk-based authentication?

options.A: Allow access, because the password was correct
options.B: Ask for the answer to a stored security question
options.C: Ask for a passkey from the lecturer's enrolled phone
options.D: Block the attempt and lock the lecturer's account for review

questions.key_concept: Risk-based authentication scales the check to the risk: a medium score triggers a stronger factor, not a lockout.
questions.pre_read: Note what is normal and what is new about this sign-in attempt.
questions.correct_explanation: Risk-based authentication matches the check to the risk. Low risk passes, medium risk asks for a stronger factor and high risk is blocked for review. A right password on an unfamiliar laptop is medium, so a passkey from the enrolled phone fits. Blocking and locking the account is the runner-up: it treats a common, explainable change as an attack and locks out a genuine user.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the password matched. But a stolen password matches too; the unfamiliar laptop is exactly the signal the score exists to act on.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it adds a step. But a security question is another thing you know, and its answers are often guessable or public.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: caution feels safe. But blocking and locking is the response to high risk; a new laptop alone calls for more proof, not a lockout.

tips: Eliminate: A treats a matching password as enough despite the risk signal, and B adds a second, often guessable thing you know rather than a stronger factor.
Final two: C beats D because medium risk calls for more proof; blocking and locking is for high risk and locks out a genuine user.
Exam cue: adaptive authentication steps up proof as risk rises: pass, then ask for a stronger factor, then block for review.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 IA-10 (Adaptive Authentication)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'adaptive authentication asks for stronger proof as the risk score rises' (notes 3.1.8 Adaptive Authentication and AI Behavior Analysis). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 2, 30 Oct 2026.

questions.question: A company's IT manager wants one system to run access requests, approvals and periodic reviews for every employee's application access, with records kept. Which tool type BEST fits?

options.A: An identity governance and administration (IGA) platform
options.B: A directory service that holds users and groups
options.C: A privileged access management (PAM) vault
options.D: A security information and event management (SIEM) system

questions.key_concept: IGA platforms run access requests, approvals and reviews for everyone; PAM guards privileged accounts; directories store identities.
questions.pre_read: List the jobs the stem asks for, then check which tool does all of them for every employee.
questions.correct_explanation: Identity governance and administration (IGA) runs the life cycle around access: requests, approvals, provisioning and periodic reviews, with a record of each decision. A privileged access management (PAM) vault is the runner-up because it also approves and logs access, but only for administrator accounts and their secrets, not every employee's everyday application access.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the directory is where accounts live. But it stores users and groups; it does not run requests, approvals or reviews.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: PAM tools approve and log access too. But they guard administrator accounts and secrets, not every employee's everyday application access.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it keeps detailed records. But a SIEM collects and correlates security logs; it does not request, approve or review access.

tips: Eliminate: B stores accounts but runs no approvals or reviews, and D collects security logs rather than managing access.
Final two: A beats C because IGA covers everyone's access; PAM focuses on administrator accounts and their secrets.
Exam cue: match the tool to the job: a directory stores identities, IGA governs requests and reviews, PAM guards admin access, a SIEM watches logs.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-2 (Account Management); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-2(1) (Account Management | Automated System Account Management)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'identity governance tools run requests, approvals and reviews for all users' (notes 3.1.13 IAM Frameworks and Tools). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 2, 30 Oct 2026.

questions.subtopic: 3.1 Identity life cycle. Federated and guest access
questions.question: A university lets a partner college's researchers sign in to its lab-booking system with their own college accounts. Which statement is MOST accurate for the university's IT team?

options.A: The researchers need no access reviews, since the college employs them
options.B: The college decides what each researcher may do in the system
options.C: The university's system now stores each researcher's college password
options.D: The university decides what each researcher may do in the system

questions.key_concept: Federation lets a partner prove who a user is; the resource owner still decides, limits and removes that user's access.
questions.pre_read: Picture a researcher signing in, and trace which organization checks what.
questions.correct_explanation: In federation, the partner's identity provider proves who the user is; the resource owner still decides what that user may do. So the university sets, limits and removes the researchers' rights in its own system. The college deciding is the runner-up: it vouches for identity and should report leavers, but it does not authorize access to the university's resources.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the college manages its own staff. But the risk sits on the university's system, so outside users still need sponsors, end dates and reviews.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the college does vouch for its researchers. But federation passes on who the user is; the university still decides what they may do.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the researchers do sign in. But the college checks the password; the university's system receives a signed assertion, never the password.

tips: Eliminate: A skips reviews for outside users, and C misreads federation, which never hands the password to the system.
Final two: D beats B because federation shares identity, not permission; the system's owner still authorizes.
Exam cue: in federation, the home organization answers 'who is this?' and the resource owner answers 'what may they do?'
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-63C-4 Section 3.8 (RP Subscriber Accounts: access rights are kept at the relying party); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-3 (Access Enforcement)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'federation passes on identity while the resource owner keeps authorization' (notes 3.1.15 Third-Party, Guest and Federated Access). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 2, 30 Oct 2026.

questions.question: An attacker stole a session cookie from a payroll portal that keeps staff signed in all day after multifactor sign-in, then changed bank details. Which control should the portal team add as BEST?

options.A: Require longer passwords at every sign-in to the portal
options.B: Require a fresh sign-in before sensitive changes are saved
options.C: Remind staff to close the browser tab after making changes
options.D: Shorten the idle timeout for signed-in staff to 15 minutes

questions.key_concept: Reauthentication before sensitive actions stops attackers who steal an already signed-in session.
questions.pre_read: Note what the attacker actually stole, and which checks that theft lets them skip.
questions.correct_explanation: Strong sign-in protects only the start of a session; a stolen cookie skips it. Asking for a fresh sign-in before sensitive changes means the attacker, who holds the cookie but not the factors, is stopped at the step that matters. A shorter idle timeout is the runner-up: it shrinks the window, but a cookie replayed while the session is live, then kept busy, is never timed out.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because stronger sign-in feels safer. But the attacker never signed in; they reused a session that was already authenticated.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it sounds like signing out. But closing a tab often leaves the session valid until it times out or is revoked.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: idle timeouts suit unattended screens. But a cookie replayed while the session is live, then kept busy, never goes idle, so the change still goes through.

tips: Eliminate: A strengthens a sign-in the attacker skipped, and C relies on closing a tab, which often leaves the session valid.
Final two: B beats D because a fresh sign-in stops a stolen session at the sensitive step; an idle timeout misses a session kept active.
Exam cue: when a session can be hijacked, guard the high-risk action itself with reauthentication; timeouts only shorten the window.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 IA-11 (Re-authentication); NIST SP 800-63B-4 Section 6.4 (Session Attacks: hijacking after an authentication event)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'ask users to sign in again before sensitive actions' (notes 3.1.16 Sessions, Timeouts and Reauthentication). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 2, 30 Oct 2026.

questions.question: A new hire arrives at a bank branch for a laptop and first sign-in details. Which check BEST lets the IT technician confirm the new hire is the person in the human resources record?

options.A: Check the offer letter the person brings against the record
options.B: Ask them to state their manager's name and start date
options.C: Compare a government photo ID with the person and the record
options.D: Text a code to the mobile number they give at the desk

questions.key_concept: Identity proofing validates evidence and ties it to the person presenting it, such as by comparing a photo ID with their face.
questions.pre_read: For each check, ask whether an impostor holding the right papers or facts could pass it.
questions.correct_explanation: Identity proofing must tie the evidence to the person standing there. A government photo ID, compared with their face and with the human resources record, does both. The offer letter is the runner-up: it matches the record, but it carries no photo, so anyone holding it could claim to be the new hire.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the letter matches the record. But it has no photo, so it proves only that someone is holding the letter.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because only the real hire should know these facts. But such details are often guessable or public, and knowledge questions are not accepted proof of identity.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because codes feel secure. But the number came from the claimant, so the code proves they hold a phone, not who they are.

tips: Eliminate: B relies on facts others can find, and D sends a code to a number the claimant chose.
Final two: C beats A because a photo ID links the evidence to the face in front of you; a letter can be carried by anyone.
Exam cue: proofing asks two things: is the evidence genuine, and does it belong to the person presenting it?
