questions.question: An ambulance service tightens fingerprint sign-in on its crews' patient-record tablets so impostors are almost never accepted. Which side effect should the IT team MOST expect?

options.A: More genuine crew members turned away by the reader
options.B: Fewer repeat scans needed by genuine crew members
options.C: A higher crossover error rate for each reader
options.D: Copied fingerprints no longer working for attackers

questions.key_concept: Tightening a biometric threshold lowers false acceptances but raises false rejections; the two errors trade against each other.
questions.pre_read: Picture both kinds of people at a tablet: crew members and impostors.
questions.correct_explanation: Every biometric reader trades two errors. Lowering false acceptances (false matches), where an impostor matches, raises false rejections (false non-matches), where a genuine crew member fails to match. So crews will be turned away more often and need a quick fallback during a call. Expecting copied fingerprints to fail is the runner-up: the threshold judges ordinary impostors, while stopping fakes needs presentation attack detection.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a stricter reader sounds more accurate. But tightening works the other way: genuine fingers that matched before now fall short, so crews need more repeat scans.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it names a real biometric measure. But the crossover rate is where both errors meet for a reader; moving the threshold does not change it.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: a stricter reader sounds harder to fool. But a good copy of an enrolled fingerprint still matches; spotting fakes needs presentation attack detection, such as liveness checks.

tips: Eliminate: B reverses the trade-off, since a stricter match sends genuine users back to rescan, and C confuses a reader's fixed crossover point with its threshold setting.
Final two: A beats D because the threshold sets how close a match must be; copied fingerprints are stopped by presentation attack detection, not by tightening.
Exam cue: biometrics balance false acceptance against false rejection. Push one down and the other rises, so plan a fallback for genuine users.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-63B-4 Section 3.2.3 (Use of Biometrics: false match and false non-match rates)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'biometric thresholds trade false acceptances against false rejections' (notes 3.1.4 Authentication Factors and MFA). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 2, 30 Oct 2026. Standards audit fix (30 Oct 2026): runner-up is D (copied prints), B no longer falls on an absolute, terms match the cited source.

questions.question: A staff member who signs in with a passkey clicks an email link to a look-alike sign-in page. What MOST accurately explains why the attacker gets nothing reusable?

options.A: The passkey's code changes every 30 seconds, so a stolen one expires
options.B: The passkey is longer than any password, so it cannot be guessed
options.C: The passkey sends its private key encrypted to the genuine site
options.D: The passkey answers only requests from the genuine site's domain

questions.key_concept: Passkeys resist phishing because each sign-in is bound to the genuine site's address, and the private key is never sent to any site.
questions.pre_read: Think about what a look-alike page could capture and pass on to the real site.
questions.correct_explanation: A passkey's private key is never sent to any website. It signs a challenge only for the site the passkey was registered with, after the browser checks the site's address, so a look-alike domain gets no valid response to relay. Sending the private key encrypted is the runner-up: it sounds secure, but the site only ever receives a signature, never the key.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because one-time codes do expire. But passkeys use no typed codes, and a relayed code can still be used within its 30 seconds.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because long secrets resist guessing. But phishing captures secrets rather than guessing them; length alone would not stop a relay.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: it sounds like strong protection. But a passkey never sends its private key to any site; the real site receives only a signed answer bound to its address.

tips: Eliminate: A describes one-time codes, which a look-alike page can relay in time, and B answers guessing, not phishing.
Final two: D beats C because the private key is never sent to a site; what protects the user is a signature bound to the real site's address.
Exam cue: phishing-resistant means bound to the genuine site. If a fake page can pass on what the user types or approves, it is not phishing-resistant.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-63B-4 (Authentication and Authenticator Management: phishing resistance); NIST SP 800-63B-4 Section 3.2.5.2 (Verifier Name Binding)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'passkeys bind each sign-in to the genuine site and keep the private key on the device' (notes 3.1.5 Phishing-Resistant MFA and Passkeys). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 2, 30 Oct 2026. Standards audit fix (30 Oct 2026): synced passkeys can leave the device, so the item now rests on the key never being sent to a site.

questions.question: An online bookshop's developer proposes storing customer passwords encrypted, so support staff can read forgotten ones back to customers. Which approach should the security analyst recommend as BEST?

options.A: Encrypt the passwords with a key held by the support lead
options.B: Store salted, slow hashes and offer a verified password reset
options.C: Encode the passwords in Base64 so they look unreadable
options.D: Hash the passwords with a fast hash to keep sign-in quick

questions.key_concept: Store passwords as salted, slow hashes and reset forgotten ones; never keep them in a form that can be read back.
questions.pre_read: Ask what an attacker who steals the stored passwords could do under each option.
questions.correct_explanation: Anything that can be decrypted can be stolen and read, so passwords are stored as salted hashes, using a slow hashing scheme that makes each guess costly. A forgotten password is replaced through a verified reset, never read back. Encrypting with a closely held key is the runner-up: it limits who can decrypt, but a stolen key or an insider still exposes every password.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: a closely held key limits access. But whoever steals the key, or the lead themselves, can still read every password.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the stored text looks scrambled. But Base64 is encoding, not encryption; anyone can reverse it instantly without a key.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because hashes cannot be reversed. But fast hashes let attackers test enormous numbers of guesses quickly after stealing the file.

tips: Eliminate: C uses reversible encoding, not protection, and D picks a fast hash that makes stolen hashes quick to crack.
Final two: B beats A because hashes cannot be turned back into passwords; anything encrypted can be decrypted by whoever gets the key.
Exam cue: passwords are never recovered, only reset. Store them salted and slow-hashed so a stolen file is costly to crack.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-63B-4 (Authentication and Authenticator Management: password requirements); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 IA-5(1) (Authenticator Management | Password-based Authentication)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'store passwords as salted, slow hashes and reset rather than recover them' (notes 3.1.6 Passwords and Modern Password Standards). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 2, 30 Oct 2026.

questions.question: A school's developer is adding 'Sign in with your school account' to a homework app, which must learn who each student is. What should the security analyst advise as BEST?

options.A: Use OpenID Connect and verify the ID token it returns
options.B: Use an OAuth 2.0 access token as proof of identity
options.C: Treat each student's school email address as proof of identity
options.D: Have students type their school password into the app

questions.key_concept: OpenID Connect proves who a user is with a signed ID token; OAuth 2.0 alone grants access to data, not identity.
questions.pre_read: Focus on what the app needs to learn, and which option actually gives it that.
questions.correct_explanation: OpenID Connect (OIDC) adds identity to OAuth 2.0: the school's identity provider signs an ID token saying who the student is, and the app checks it. An OAuth 2.0 access token alone is the runner-up: it lets an app reach data on a user's behalf, but it is not built to prove who the user is.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: OpenID Connect is built on OAuth 2.0. But an access token grants limited access to data; it is not designed to prove who the user is.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because each address belongs to one student. But an address is only a claim; anyone can type it, so it proves nothing on its own.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it checks a real password. But federated sign-in exists so the app never sees the password; collecting it invites theft.

tips: Eliminate: D hands the password to the app, which federation avoids, and C treats a claimed address as proof.
Final two: A beats B because the ID token proves who signed in; an OAuth access token only grants access to data.
Exam cue: OAuth 2.0 grants access; OpenID Connect adds identity on top. For 'who is this user?', look for OpenID Connect or SAML.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-63C-4 Section 3.12.3 (Identity APIs: the ID Token is the assertion and an OAuth 2.0 access token reaches the API)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'OpenID Connect proves identity while OAuth 2.0 grants access' (notes 3.1.7 Single Sign-On and Federation). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 2, 30 Oct 2026.

questions.question: A claims handler at an insurer moves to underwriting, and the claims manager asks that they keep claims access for two weeks to hand over open files. What is the access analyst's BEST action?

options.A: Keep the claims access until the handler confirms handovers are done
options.B: Ask the underwriting manager to approve keeping the old access
options.C: Record the claims access as temporary, with an end date
options.D: Keep the claims access, since both teams belong to the insurer

questions.key_concept: When a mover needs old access for a handover, grant it as approved, temporary access that expires on a set date.
questions.pre_read: Note what the claims manager asked for and for how long.
questions.correct_explanation: Handover access is a real need, but it must be approved for a set period and then expire, or the mover keeps old rights indefinitely. Recording it as temporary with a two-week end date meets the need and removes it automatically. Keeping it until the handler says they are done is the runner-up: it depends on someone remembering, and leftover access tends to stay.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: it allows for handovers. But with no end date, removal depends on someone remembering, and leftover rights become privilege creep.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the new manager approves new access. But the claims manager decides about claims access, and this keeps the old access with no end date.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because both teams sit inside one company. But access follows the job, not the employer; old rights the new job does not need should go.

tips: Eliminate: D ties access to the employer instead of the job, and B asks the wrong manager to approve old access with no end date.
Final two: C beats A because an end date removes the access automatically; waiting for the handler's word lets it linger.
Exam cue: movers lose old access at the move. If a handover needs some of it, grant it as temporary access with an end date.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 PS-5 (Personnel Transfer); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-2 (Account Management)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'handover access for a mover is approved separately and expires' (notes 3.1.9 Movers and Privilege Creep). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 2, 30 Oct 2026.

questions.question: A departing developer owns the service account a nightly sales report uses, and knows its password; the report must keep running. What should the IT technician arrange as BEST?

options.A: Write the password into the handover notes for the team
options.B: Disable the service account along with the developer's own account
options.C: Leave the service account alone, since nobody signs in with it
options.D: Assign the account a new owner, who then changes its password

questions.key_concept: A leaver's service accounts need a new owner and changed secrets if still needed, or retirement if not.
questions.pre_read: Note the two facts about the service account, and weigh each option against both.
questions.correct_explanation: A service account outlives its owner's job, so it needs a new named owner. Because the developer knows the password, the new owner changes it, so the leaver's knowledge stops working. Disabling it is the runner-up: it would close the risk, but it breaks a report the business still needs; retiring an account is right only when nothing needs it.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the team will need it. But a password in shared notes spreads the secret further; it belongs in a vault with a named owner.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: removing the leaver's access is the goal. But the report must keep running, so disabling breaks it; a new owner and new password close the risk instead.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because no person signs in with it. But the developer still knows a working password, and ownerless service accounts are a favorite target.

tips: Eliminate: C leaves a password the leaver knows working, and A spreads the secret instead of protecting it.
Final two: D beats B because the report must keep running; a new owner and new password remove the leaver's access without breaking it.
Exam cue: when someone leaves, check what they owned and knew, not just their own login. Reassign and rotate what is still needed; retire the rest.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-2 (Account Management); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 IA-5 (Authenticator Management)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'a leaver's service accounts are reassigned and rotated, or retired' (notes 3.1.11 Deprovisioning Leavers; 3.1.12 Non-Human Identities Through the Life Cycle). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 2, 30 Oct 2026.

questions.question: A council's role-based system has 380 roles for 400 staff, mostly one-offs created for single requests, though staff fall into about 15 job types. Which fix should the access analyst propose as BEST?

options.A: Consolidate into standard roles, adding time-limited extras
options.B: Keep the custom roles and review each one yearly
options.C: Replace the roles with attribute-based access control
options.D: Let managers edit their own team's roles whenever needed

questions.key_concept: Role-based access control works when roles mirror jobs; one-off needs are temporary requests, not new custom roles.
questions.pre_read: Compare the number of roles with the number of job types, and ask what that gap means.
questions.correct_explanation: Role-based access control works when roles match jobs; hundreds of one-off roles defeat it and make reviews and moves hard. With about 15 job types, rebuilding job roles and handling one-off needs as time-limited requests restores order. Attribute-based control is the runner-up: it answers role explosion caused by many changing conditions, such as location or training, but these roles came from single requests.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because reviews catch excess access. But reviewing 380 near-duplicate roles each year is the burden sprawl creates; it leaves the sprawl in place.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: attribute-based control is a known remedy for role explosion. But it suits changing conditions; these roles came from single requests, and access follows 15 job types.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because managers know their teams. But unreviewed edits by each manager are how roles multiplied, and no owner checks them for conflicts.

tips: Eliminate: D keeps the unchecked edits that caused the sprawl, and B reviews the 380 roles instead of reducing them.
Final two: A beats C because access here follows job type, which is what roles express; attribute rules add complexity this case does not need.
Exam cue: when roles outnumber jobs, rebuild roles around jobs and handle one-off needs as time-limited requests.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-3(7) (Access Enforcement | Role-based Access Control); CIS Controls v8.1 Safeguard 6.8 (Define and Maintain Role-Based Access Control)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'roles should mirror jobs, with one-off needs handled as temporary requests' (notes 3.2.7 Role-Based Access Control (RBAC)). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 2, 30 Oct 2026. Standards audit fix (30 Oct 2026): stem now says why the roles exist, so attribute-based control is no longer defensible; B is no longer a strawman.

questions.question: A junior network administrator finds 140 allow rules, many with no recorded purpose, on the firewall guarding a clinic's lab systems, which the network manager owns. What should the administrator do FIRST?

options.A: Move the unexplained rules to the end of the rule list
options.B: Write a purpose for each rule from its recent traffic logs
options.C: List the rules and ask the manager to arrange a review
options.D: Disable the unexplained rules now, then tell the manager

questions.key_concept: Access rules pile up over time; each needs an owner, a purpose and periodic review, arranged through the system's owner.
questions.pre_read: Note what the administrator found and who owns the device.
questions.correct_explanation: Rules pile up, and each needs an owner, a purpose and a periodic review. The administrator's part is to document the rules and bring them to the firewall's owner, who can arrange a review with each business area. Disabling unexplained rules is the runner-up: they may look unused, but some may carry live lab traffic, and changing the firewall is the owner's decision, made through change control.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because rules at the end are matched last. But reordering an owned firewall's rules is still a change; it can break live lab traffic and skips the owner.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because recorded purposes are the goal. But traffic shows what a rule carries, not why it should exist; only the owner can confirm each purpose.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: unexplained rules are a real risk. But some may carry live lab traffic, and changes to an owned firewall go through its owner and change control.

tips: Eliminate: A reorders an owned firewall's rules without change control, and B guesses purposes from traffic that only the owner can confirm.
Final two: C beats D because the manager owns the firewall; the administrator documents and raises the issue rather than changing live rules alone.
Exam cue: every access rule needs an owner, a purpose and a review. Report rule sprawl to the owner; do not clean it up alone.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-41 Rev. 1 Section 5.5 (Manage: review the firewall policy regularly to find rules no longer needed); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CM-3 (Configuration Change Control)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'each access rule needs an owner, a purpose and periodic review' (notes 3.2.9 Rule-Based Access Control). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 2, 30 Oct 2026. Standards audit fix (30 Oct 2026): asset moved away from cc_d5_041's payroll firewall.

questions.question: A 30-person design agency gives staff access by job, and its owner wants to switch to mandatory access control because it is the strictest model. What should the security analyst advise as BEST?

options.A: Use mandatory access control, because the strictest model is the safest
options.B: Use role-based access control, because each job maps to one role
options.C: Use rule-based access control, because one rule can cover every job
options.D: Use discretionary access control, because owners know their own files best

questions.key_concept: Choose an access control model that fits the data and the organization; the strictest model is not automatically the best.
questions.pre_read: Note what the agency handles and how access works today, then judge each model's fit.
questions.correct_explanation: The best model fits the data and the organization, not the strictest one available. A design agency whose access already follows jobs suits role-based access control. Mandatory access control is the runner-up: it is strong, but its central labels and clearances are rigid and costly, built for classified data, and would slow a small creative team for little gain.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: mandatory control is the strictest. But labels and clearances are rigid and costly, suited to classified data, not a small agency's artwork.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because rules are simple. But one rule applies to everyone alike, so it cannot give designers and accountants different access.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because owners know their files. But discretionary control lets each owner share at will, inviting oversharing, and moves away from job-based access.

tips: Eliminate: D hands access decisions to each owner, inviting oversharing, and C applies one condition to everyone, so it cannot reflect different jobs.
Final two: B beats A because the model should fit the data and size; mandatory control's labels suit classified data, not a design agency.
Exam cue: choose the model by who should decide and what the data needs; the strictest model is not automatically the best.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-3(7) (Access Enforcement | Role-based Access Control); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-3(3) (Access Enforcement | Mandatory Access Control)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'choose the model that fits the data and organization, not the strictest' (notes 3.2.10 Choosing an Access Control Model). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 2, 30 Oct 2026.

questions.question: A school's IT technician must give 25 new teachers edit access to the shared lesson-plan folder. Which approach is BEST?

options.A: Grant each teacher edit rights on the folder one by one
options.B: Share the folder with everyone so no teacher is missed
options.C: Give the teachers one shared login that has the folder rights
options.D: Add the teachers to a group that holds the folder rights

questions.key_concept: Grant permissions to groups or roles and manage membership, so access stays easy to review and remove.
questions.pre_read: Think ahead to the day one of these teachers leaves, and what each option leaves behind.
questions.correct_explanation: Permissions are best granted to groups, not individuals. Adding the teachers to a group that holds the folder rights gives the same access, and when a teacher leaves or changes job, removing them from the group removes the access. Granting rights one by one is the runner-up: it works today, but 25 separate entries are hard to review and easy to leave behind.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: it gives the right access today. But 25 separate entries are hard to review, and each must be found and removed when a teacher moves.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because nobody is left out. But everyone includes pupils, office staff and visitors, far beyond the teachers who need the folder.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because one login is quick to set up. But a shared login hides which teacher made each change and cannot be removed for one person.

tips: Eliminate: B opens the folder to far more people than need it, and C puts every teacher on one login that cannot show who acted.
Final two: D beats A because group membership is easy to review and remove; individual grants pile up and get missed.
Exam cue: grant rights to groups or roles, then manage who belongs. It keeps reviews and removals simple.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-2 (Account Management); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-3 (Access Enforcement)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'grant permissions to groups or roles rather than individuals' (notes 3.2.1 Logical Access Controls and Access Decisions). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 2, 30 Oct 2026.

questions.question: At a tax office, case officers can open any taxpayer's file, and one officer browsed a famous athlete's file with no assigned case. Which change should the office manager make to BEST prevent this?

options.A: Limit each officer to files for their assigned cases
options.B: Remove the officers' rights to edit any file
options.C: Log each file viewed and check it against assigned cases monthly
options.D: Require multifactor sign-in before officers open any file

questions.key_concept: Need to know limits each person to the information their current work requires, preventing curiosity browsing.
questions.pre_read: Picture the same officer trying the same lookup after each change.
questions.correct_explanation: Need to know limits each person to the information their current work requires. Tying access to assigned cases stops browsing before it happens. Logging views and checking them against assigned cases is the runner-up: it would catch the officer afterward and deters misuse, but the athlete's privacy is already breached by then.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it limits what officers can do. But browsing is reading, so officers without edit rights can still view every file.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: logging deters and detects browsing. But it acts after the file has been seen, and the goal is to prevent it.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it strengthens access. But it proves who the officer is; it does not limit which files they may open.

tips: Eliminate: B limits changes, not viewing, and D strengthens sign-in without limiting which files open.
Final two: A beats C because it stops the browsing before it happens; logs only reveal it afterward.
Exam cue: need to know asks whether this person's current work requires this data. When asked to prevent, pick the preventive control over the detective one.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-6 (Least Privilege); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-3 (Access Enforcement)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'need to know limits people to the data their current work requires' (notes 3.2.2 Least Privilege and Need to Know). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 2, 30 Oct 2026.

questions.question: At a water utility, two operators staff each shift, and either can change chlorine dosing from the control room; a wrong level could harm the public. Which control should the plant manager add as BEST?

options.A: Require a longer password for the operator's account
options.B: Log each dosing change and alert the supervisor
options.C: Require a second operator to confirm each dosing change
options.D: Rotate dosing duties among the operators every week

questions.key_concept: Two-person control requires a second authorized person to confirm a high-impact action before it takes effect.
questions.pre_read: Note what could happen to people if one wrong change went through.
questions.correct_explanation: When a single wrong action could hurt people, a second authorized person should confirm it before it takes effect: two-person control. Logging with an alert is the runner-up: it records who acted and brings help quickly, but it works after the chlorine level has changed, when harm may already be under way. Prevention comes first where public safety is at stake.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it strengthens sign-in. But it proves who the operator is; it does not stop that operator acting alone.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: alerts bring a fast response. But they fire after the level changes, and harm to the public may already have started.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because job rotation is a real control. But it helps uncover misuse over time; on any given shift, one operator can still make a harmful change alone.

tips: Eliminate: D changes who acts alone rather than adding a second person, and A strengthens sign-in without stopping a lone change.
Final two: C beats B because confirmation happens before the change takes effect; an alert comes after people may already be at risk.
Exam cue: for high-impact actions, especially where safety is at stake, require a second person before the action, not a log after it.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-3(2) (Access Enforcement | Dual Authorization); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-5 (Separation of Duties)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'two-person control for high-impact actions where safety is at stake' (notes 3.2.3 Separation of Duties and Two-Person Control). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 2, 30 Oct 2026. Standards audit fix (30 Oct 2026): stem says two operators staff each shift; D is no longer a strawman; neutral subtopic.

questions.question: A TV broadcaster's vendor engineer will upgrade its playout server remotely and unsupervised, with administrator rights. Which control should the system administrator set up to BEST show the owner exactly what the engineer did?

options.A: Log when the engineer's admin account signs in and out
options.B: Record the engineer's session in the privileged access tool
options.C: Ask the engineer for a written summary of every change
options.D: Let the engineer use the IT team's shared admin account

questions.key_concept: Privileged sessions, especially by outsiders, should be brokered and recorded so the owner can see exactly what was done.
questions.pre_read: Ask what evidence each option would give the owner the next morning.
questions.correct_explanation: Privileged access management can broker an outsider's admin session and record it, so the owner can replay exactly what was done. Logging sign-in and sign-out is the runner-up: it shows when the engineer was on the server, but not which commands they ran or which settings they changed.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: it shows when the engineer was connected. But sign-in times reveal nothing about which commands or settings were changed.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the engineer knows what they did. But a self-written summary can leave things out; it is not independent evidence.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it is quick to arrange. But a shared account hides who acted, so the engineer's actions mix with the IT team's.

tips: Eliminate: C relies on the engineer's own account of events, and D mixes the engineer's actions into a shared login.
Final two: B beats A because a session recording shows what was done; sign-in logs show only when someone arrived and left.
Exam cue: for privileged work, especially by outsiders, record the session itself; sign-in records prove presence, not actions.

questions.question: A publishing house's project lead gives an editor full control of a manuscripts folder to revise, and the editor reshares it with a freelancer. Which change should the project lead make to BEST prevent this?

options.A: Ask the freelancer to confirm they deleted the manuscripts
options.B: Give the editor read access in place of full control
options.C: Share the folder by link instead of by name
options.D: Give the editor edit rights that do not include sharing

questions.key_concept: Under discretionary access control, holders of full control can pass access on, so grant only the rights each person needs.
questions.pre_read: Trace how the manuscripts reached the freelancer, step by step.
questions.correct_explanation: Under discretionary access control, whoever holds full control can pass access on. Edit rights without the right to share let the editor do the job while sharing decisions stay with the owner. Read access is the runner-up: it would stop the reshare, but an editor must change the manuscripts, so it blocks the work the access exists for.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it seems to undo the share. But copies may already exist, and nothing stops the next onward share.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: read access would stop the reshare. But the editor must change the manuscripts, so read access blocks their job; edit rights without sharing fit it.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because links feel tidy. But anyone who obtains a link can open the folder, which widens sharing instead of limiting it.

tips: Eliminate: A tries to undo one share after the fact, and C widens access to anyone holding the link.
Final two: D beats B because the editor needs to change the manuscripts; edit rights without sharing fit the job, while read access blocks it.
Exam cue: in discretionary access control, full control includes passing access on. Grant the rights the job needs, and keep sharing with the owner.

questions.question: Under mandatory access control, an analyst cleared to Top Secret is refused a Top Secret file belonging to another program. What MOST likely explains the refusal?

options.A: The analyst's clearance must be one level above the label
options.B: The file's owner has not shared it with the analyst
options.C: The file's compartment requires a need to know the analyst lacks
options.D: Top Secret files need the security officer to open them

questions.key_concept: Mandatory access control needs both a sufficient clearance and a need to know, often enforced through compartments.
questions.pre_read: Note what the analyst holds and what the file belongs to.
questions.correct_explanation: Under mandatory access control, clearance is necessary but not sufficient. Files are often placed in compartments, and the system also checks that the person has a need to know for that compartment, so a Top Secret clearance alone does not open another program's work. The owner not sharing is the runner-up: owner choice is how discretionary control works; under mandatory control, owners cannot grant access at will.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because higher sounds safer. But a clearance equal to the label is enough; the extra check is need to know, not a higher level.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: someone did withhold access. But owner choice is discretionary control; under mandatory control, central labels and need to know decide, not the owner.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because Top Secret sounds reserved for officers. But cleared staff with a need to know can open such files; the officer manages labels.

tips: Eliminate: A invents a rule that clearance must exceed the label, and D wrongly reserves Top Secret files for the security officer.
Final two: C beats B because mandatory control checks label, clearance and need to know; owners do not decide.
Exam cue: under mandatory access control, a matching clearance is necessary but not enough; need to know, often by compartment, is the second test.

questions.question: A firm's attribute-based policy opens sales files only to staff whose department attribute is Sales, yet a worker who moved to finance weeks ago still opens them. Which cause should the analyst MOST suspect?

options.A: The worker still holds a Sales role in the directory
options.B: The department attribute at its source still says Sales
options.C: The policy checked the department attribute once, at account creation
options.D: The worker's multifactor sign-in was not re-enrolled after the move

questions.key_concept: Attribute-based access control is only as accurate as its attributes; a stale value at the source gives a wrong decision.
questions.pre_read: Note exactly what the policy checks, then ask where that value comes from.
questions.correct_explanation: Attribute-based control decides each request from current attribute values, so it is only as accurate as its attributes. If the attribute's source, such as the human resources record, still lists Sales, the policy correctly applies to a wrong value and grants access. A leftover Sales role is the runner-up: it would matter under role-based control, but this policy checks the department attribute, not roles.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: leftover roles often cause privilege creep. But this policy checks the department attribute, not role membership, so a role alone would not open the files.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because some attributes are set at hiring. But attribute-based control evaluates attributes on every request, so changes should take effect.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the worker's situation changed. But sign-in proves identity; it does not decide which files the policy allows.

tips: Eliminate: C misdescribes the model, which checks attributes on each request, and D confuses sign-in with the access decision.
Final two: B beats A because the policy reads the department attribute; a stale value grants access whatever roles say.
Exam cue: attribute-based decisions are only as good as their attributes. When access is wrong but the policy is right, suspect stale data at the source.

questions.subtopic: 3.2 Logical access. Automated systems and AI agents
questions.question: A firm's AI assistant answers staff questions by searching all file shares through its own all-access account, so interns can get answers drawn from payroll files. Which fix should the security analyst propose as BEST?

options.A: Limit it to files that the person asking can already open
options.B: Require interns to use multifactor sign-in before asking it
options.C: Block any answer that mentions salaries or other payroll terms
options.D: Keep its access, since reading files changes nothing

questions.key_concept: An AI assistant acting for a user should reach only what that user may access; filtering output does not fix excess access.
questions.pre_read: Trace how payroll details reached an intern, step by step.
questions.correct_explanation: An AI assistant should never reach more than the person it is acting for. Limiting each search to files the asking person can already open closes the gap. Blocking payroll words is the runner-up: it hides one obvious leak, but other sensitive files, and differently worded answers, still pass through the all-access account.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it strengthens sign-in. But it confirms who the intern is; it does not limit which files the assistant searches for them.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: it hides the most obvious leak. But word filters miss other sensitive files and rephrased answers, and the all-access account remains.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because reading changes nothing. But reading is exactly how payroll data reached interns; read access to everything breaks least privilege.

tips: Eliminate: D treats read-only access as harmless, and B strengthens sign-in without limiting what the assistant can reach.
Final two: A beats C because it removes the excess access itself; a word filter only masks some of what the account can still reach.
Exam cue: an AI agent acting for a user should never reach more than that user can. Fix the access, not just the output.

questions.question: A retailer's administrators all sign in through single sign-on (SSO), and the IT manager wants an emergency account for when SSO itself fails. Which setup should the security analyst propose as BEST?

options.A: Assign it to the IT manager as a second everyday admin account
options.B: Give it a strong password that rotates monthly
options.C: Protect it with SSO and multifactor sign-in like other admins
options.D: Keep its credentials sealed offline and alert on each use

questions.key_concept: Break-glass accounts must work when normal sign-in fails: sealed credentials, few holders, regular tests and an alert on every use.
questions.pre_read: Note what the emergency account is for, and what each setup depends on.
questions.correct_explanation: A break-glass account must work when normal sign-in fails, so it cannot depend on SSO. Its credentials are sealed offline, such as in a safe,, held by few people and tested regularly, and every use raises an alert and a review. Putting it behind SSO with multifactor sign-in is the runner-up: that suits daily admin accounts, but it would fail in exactly the outage it exists for.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because one named person is accountable. But daily use exposes it to the same attacks as normal accounts; an emergency account stays unused until needed.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because rotation sounds safe. But routine rotation misses its purpose: few should hold it, it stays sealed, and every use raises an alert.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: strong sign-in suits admin accounts. But if it depends on SSO, it fails in the very outage it exists for; use a strong factor that works without SSO.

tips: Eliminate: A turns the emergency account into an everyday one, and B treats it like any admin account instead of sealing it and watching its use.
Final two: D beats C because the account must work when SSO fails; tying it to SSO defeats its purpose.
Exam cue: break-glass access is sealed, independent of the system that might fail, tested, and alerts on every use.
